To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

MHC class II (MII) expression restricted to CD11c+CD8α+ dendritc cells (DCs) and CD11bDCs is sufficient to control L. major infection, and that MII expression in these cells, but not in macrophages, B cells, or Langerhans Cells (LCs), is sufficient for Th1 differentiation and parasite control.
MHC class II–expressing CD11b+ or CD8α+ cells are required for the development of Th1 responses to Leishmania major.
MHC II is expressed by CD11b+ DCs and CD8α + DCs and not by macrophages and Langerhans’ cells, which is sufficient to control Leishmania major infection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of antigen-presenting cells in the control of a protozoal infection.
the role of antigen-presenting cells in initiating immune responses.
understanding how the immune system controls infection with the protozoan Leishmania major (Lm) in mice.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MHC II–restricted DCs can present antigens to CD4+ T lymphocytes and initiate Th1 differentiation.
MHC II–restricted antigen presentation by DCs is sufficient to control L. major infection in the skin.
MHC II is not required for CD4+ Th1 cell differentiation or for control of a Leishmania major infection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the CD11b+ DCs, CD8α+DCs and macrophages are sufficient to control a primary Leishmania infection.
MHC class II expression on dendritic cells is sufficient for the control of Leishmania infection.
the CD4+ T helper cell 2 (Th2)–dominant immune response that occurs when MHC II is expressed by macrophages, but not by CD11b+ DCs and CD8α DCs, leads to the development of a chronic infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the MHC II–deficient mice were able to mount a Th1 immune response against Leishmania major infection.
CD11b+ conventional dendritic cells (cDCs) and CD8α+cDCs are the only cells required for the initiation of the immune response against the intracellular parasite L. major.
CD8+ dendritic cells and CD11b-positive dendritic cells can be sufficient to control a Leishmania major infection.
